To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the metabolite 3‐hydroxyglutarate is a novel fuel‐stimulated regulator of insulin secretion, and (ii) the metabolite succinate is a novel fuel sensor that regulates the activity of the Krebs cycle and insulin secretion.

1) glucose‐stimulated islet cells increase the levels of a novel class of signaling metabolites, termed “ketocycloalkylcarnitines,” which are derived from the fatty acid oxidation intermediate 2‐hydroxyglutarate, and 2) the islet cells increase levels of the signaling metabolite succinate in their fuel‐stressed compared with basal states, which is a key mechanism of islet fuel sensing.

1) the islet cell metabolome is altered by glucose in ways that are consistent with the activation of the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle and the pentose phosphate pathway, and that these pathways are important for insulin secretion, and 2) the islet metabolome is altered in type 2 diabetes in ways that are associated with reduced insulin secretion and that may provide new targets for improving insulin secretory capacity
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the islet β‐cell senses and responds to nutrients.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fuel‐stimulated state is characterized by a shift in islet cell metabolism from a state of oxidative to a state of reductive metabolism.

metabolomics has revealed 2 new mechanisms for fuel‐stimulated signaling in pancreatic β‐cells: (1) glucose‐stimulated signaling via a novel glucose sensor, the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier; and (2) a novel mechanism for insulin secretion via the β‐cell mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter.

metabolomics is a powerful new tool that will be applied to many aspects of diabetes research in the years ahead.
